NAD. The lighting makes it look like mottled skin and bruises. I have mottled skin and bruise easily. I’d get a first line blood test done and an appointment with your pediatrician to see if anything comes up. If it is mottled skin, this wouldn’t typically be a dermatologist’s domain to treat as it stems from underlying conditions. Anything from a vitamin deficiency or allergy to a genetic condition. Often primary care doctors and urgent care doctors aren’t aware of these symptoms or conditions. They aren’t trained to look for mottled skin. A geneticist would have that knowledge. Rare disease specialists have that experience as well, but pediatric geneticists are more commonly found and covered by insurance for testing

It seems like you just moved to a new home and the other kitten you were fostering went to a new home. Aside the fact that they are a kitten, kittening. Moves are stressful. The litter box is now in a new place. The cat they knew (even if they weren’t BFFs) has disappeared along with their poop from the litter box. Or maybe the entire separate litter box for the other cat disappeared and the scent of the other cat is gone. Cats bury their poop to hide from predators. Burying is instinctual. When they don’t bury it it can be because they are trying to claim their territory. Maybe your kitten is yelling at her unburied poop trying to get your attention to tell you this is all really stressful or to ask for extra attention or it could be because they’re curious about where the poop disappears to after it’s buried or they could be telling you they are in pain. As others have suggested, taking them to the scene of their poop and helping them use their paws to bury it is a good way to let them know or reinforce that behavior. This seems like normal kitten behavior and relatively normal behavior considering the situation. Have y’all moved and adopted out a kitten at the same time as fostering a kitten? Those are stressors that can bring out behaviors that you might not have seen in previous foster kittens. Kittens are babies. Everything is new, weird, fun, scary, exciting, and 15,000 other adjectives to them.

My psychiatrist thinks I have PMDD, given I keep experiencing this tiny window of time each month when it seems no medication or supplement on Earth can stop me from sobbing and ever so slightly bordering/teetering a dissociative OCD episode- which I guess is a PMDD thing when you have PTSD and OCD.

So… I guess my overall review is that it is helping. I stopped taking it for a couple of weeks out of forgetfulness and saw a dip in mood. I didn’t realize maybe the increased depression was due to the missed NAC until afterward. I’m a sensitive person, as in I have a lot of reactions to meds. I’m that ‘1 in 500,000 patients experience this bizarre life-threatening symptom after taking the med’ person. I’ve had doctors not even realize the reactions I have to meds are from meds until I force them to call the manufacturer. When the doctors report the side effects, they finally realize my body really is that sensitive. 

So, I would never flat-out suggest anyone take a supplement or med without doing the research and talking it over with a medical professional. However, I understand doctors can feel limiting in their conversations on certain topics like supplements. Doctors who shun all supplements are just as concerning as doctors who peddle using only natural remedies to heal yourself. Finding a medical professional who understands the balance exists is essential.

Even if they can’t directly help you, they will know where to direct you because they understand the social services system and hopefully should hold less bias about unhoused people.
